one_line: Camera-plus-POS exception alerts (self-checkout non-scans, back-door/receiving shrink, cash-wrap anomalies) that queue short clips for a human to review - no face recognition, no audio, no autonomous accusations.

problem.summary: Independent grocers, liquor stores, pharmacies, hardware stores and convenience stores lose roughly 1.6% of sales to shrink at industry-average rates, and the two largest buckets are internal and external theft plus process error at checkout and receiving. Self-checkout, which many stores now run, measurably raises loss (mean +22% in the year after installation across 8 grocery retailers / 1,300 stores, one of 19 before/after studies), and the loss shows up as missed scans, wrong items and walk-aways that nobody watches for because the attendant is also running customer service. Today the work is done by hand: a manager scrubs a DVR after a complaint, a receiver trusts the vendor's count, and a cashier's voids and no-sales are never compared to video. The expensive part is not cameras - it is the human attention needed to watch, and the risk of getting it wrong when a clerk acts on a hunch.

evidence.fact: US retail shrink averaged 1.6% of sales in FY2022, $112.1 billion, up from 1.4% / $93.9 billion in FY2021; internal and external theft together accounted for about 65% of shrink.
41% of surveyed retailers said no employee is authorized to stop or apprehend a shoplifter (up from 38%), so detection value now comes from documentation and deterrence rather than confrontation.

Self-checkout raised loss by a mean of 22% in the year after installation (range 3.19%-41.2%) across 8 grocery retailers / 1,300 test stores, and by +0.26 percentage points of sales across 11 grocery retailers / 1,700 test stores; both estimates come from a set of 19 before/after studies, so the 8 and 11 retailer counts are not the whole evidence base.

Missed scans were the most frequent self-checkout loss behaviour, at 1%-4.8% of transactions, in frequency data returned by 12 retailers (the overall study drew on 39 retailers with combined turnover over EUR 1 trillion).

Retailers' own estimates of how much non-scan behaviour was malicious ranged from 6% to 80%, which the authors read as evidence that intent estimates are unreliable - i.e. most alerts are not proof of theft.

Middlesex County has 2,280 retail establishments (NAICS 44-45) with 37,013 employees and average annual pay of $45,485. Within that: NAICS 4451 grocery-store industry group is 333 establishments / 7,002 employees at $32,525 average pay; NAICS 445110 supermarkets is 186 establishments / 5,902 employees at $33,172; NAICS 4453 beer-wine-liquor stores is 143 establishments / 945 employees at $30,985.

False-positive-driven accusations are a documented, government-charged harm: the FTC alleged Rite Aid's system generated thousands of false matches from 2012-2020, and employees followed, searched, ordered out or called police on wrongly flagged customers, disproportionately people of colour.

New Jersey upgraded retail-theft crimes and directed the Attorney General to 'undertake such steps as the Attorney General deems appropriate' to promote investigation, prosecution and deterrence of organised retail theft, 'which may include establishing a retail theft unit, task force, or other appropriate office or initiative' in the Department of Law and Public Safety (P.L. 2025, c.39, s.5). The creation of a unit is discretionary, not mandated by the statute; the value signal is the state's stated priority plus a statutory notification route for merchants to report retail-theft allegations to the Division of Criminal Justice.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 8-200 staff, one or more self-checkout lanes, $3M+ annual sales
buyers.why: Highest exposure to non-scan and produce PLU fraud; 186 supermarkets / 5,902 employees in Middlesex County (NAICS 445110), or 333 establishments / 7,002 employees for the wider 4451 grocery group; already has a POS and cameras, so incremental cost is analytics only.

High value per item (spirits), low staff density, single-counter layout; 143 establishments / 945 employees in the county at the lowest average pay of the retail segments checked ($30,985), so there is little budget for dedicated watchers.

OTC and high-theft SKUs plus a controlled-substance compliance culture; 198 establishments / 2,145 employees in the county at $44,480 average pay; already comfortable with camera systems and audit trails.

buyers.naics: 444140 (hardware retailers); parent industry group 4441 building material and garden equipment dealers
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-100 staff with a loading dock or back-door receiving
buyers.why: Bulky, high-ticket items and contractor traffic make receiving-count and back-door control the weak point. Middlesex County industry-group totals for 4441 are 94 establishments / 2,741 employees at $50,000 average pay; the 444140 hardware-retailer line itself reports only 13 establishments with employment withheld, so a single-store sale is the realistic unit of demand rather than a segment-wide count.

Small baskets, cash, high-turnover staff, single clerk on duty - cash-wrap voids/refunds and sweethearting are the main leaks; 96 establishments / 1,304 employees in the county at $33,022 average pay.

buyers.business_type: Small general merchandise / dollar-format variety store
buyers.why: Broad low-value assortment, self-checkout, thin staffing; 129 establishments / 7,131 employees in the county at $34,765 average pay - the segment where a chain's LP software is priced out of reach.

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Vision AI on existing checkout/self-checkout cameras plus POS data to detect non-scans, mis-scans and product switching, prompting the shopper or attendant in real time; extended to store-wide analytics (Store Intelligence) and a conversational data layer.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (no list price; the vendor's own ROI guide describes 'fees charged per lane, per week' for Evercheck)

existing_solutions.product: Self-checkout vision analytics (from the 2018 StopLift acquisition)
existing_solutions.what_it_does: StopLift's system analysed checkout video against a point-of-sale transaction feed to flag scan avoidance, items passed around the scanner and items left unscanned in the basket; NCR said it would integrate that detection into its self-checkout and store-transformation products.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (bundled with NCR self-checkout estate; deal terms not disclosed)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cloud VMS with AI people/vehicle analytics, POS overlay and alerting; the clearest public price anchor in the category. Note the pricing page states AI features and cloud archiving are not included in the $149 Professional licence, so the $548 total buys camera plus storage/licence, not the analytics.
existing_solutions.pricing: Public: $399 per camera (R120 mini dome) plus a $149 per-camera licence = $548 MSRP including hardware and licence; a $649 licence applies to the multisensor model. The page says all cameras require 'an ongoing license to operate' but does not state a billing period.

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cloud video unified with systems such as POS, marketed for faster investigations and exception review across multi-site retail and restaurants; the FAQ page describes the platform in general terms and says installation timelines vary with site size, camera needs and whether a custom POS integration is required.
Integrates POS, customer, eCommerce, inventory, video and RFID data and applies machine learning to every transaction, alert and trend to surface and rank exceptions for follow-up.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (no price shown on the platform page; quote-based)

existing_solutions.product: Local NVR with object detection, tracking, zones and a review queue
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Runs on your own hardware, defines zones and review items, records clips, integrates with Home Assistant/MQTT. Detection runs on Coral, Hailo-8/8L, OpenVINO, ONNX/TensorRT, Rockchip and other backends, and the custom-model settings take a model path plus a label map for a custom object detector, so a bespoke detector is configurable. Frigate recommends 320x320 models and crops the motion region before detection. The hard part is not the NVR, it is collecting and labelling checkout data and wiring item-level scan logic.
existing_solutions.pricing: Free/open source (Frigate itself); add-on Frigate+ hosted training is a separate subscription

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Trains models on images users upload from their own cameras, up to 12 fine tunes per annual subscription with extra fine tunes at $5; the site states only a specific set of labels is supported and that users cannot add their own custom labels yet, which rules it out for bespoke retail classes. The terms restrict use of the models to camera systems you or your organisation own or operate and expressly prohibit deploying the models at, or operating them for, sites owned or operated by your customers - commercial licences are offered separately.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (subscription price not shown in the pages opened; the site states up to 12 fine tunes per annual subscription and $5 per additional fine tune)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Detector-and-tracker toolkit for custom object/person models and zone analytics; the practical build block for a bespoke installer. Ships six trackers - BoT-SORT, ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Deep OC-SORT, FastTracker and TrackTrack - and TrackTrack is the default when no tracker is named.
existing_solutions.pricing: Public: Platform plans Free $0, Pro $29/seat/month, Enterprise custom. The licensing table lists AGPL 3.0 for the Free and Pro plans and the Enterprise licence only on the Enterprise plan, and the page states platform plans and software licences are separate - so a $29/seat/month plan does not buy a non-AGPL licence; a closed commercial deployment therefore points to the Enterprise licence (reading of the page, not legal advice).

gap_for_local_installer: The named vision-AI loss vendors sell to chains: Everseen, NCR, Agilence and Solink publish no price and are built around enterprise POS/SCO estates, while Rhombus-class cloud cameras start at $548 per camera and, at that licence tier, exclude the AI features. A 5-50 staff store in Middlesex County is too small for a chain contract and too complex for a $200 consumer kit. The open gap is a local integrator that (a) installs 4-12 cameras on a local box so no video leaves the store, (b) joins them to whatever POS the store already runs (Square, Clover, NCR, Lightspeed) using daily exports if there is no API, (c) tunes zone rules for that store's actual back door, receiving bay and cash wrap, and (d) delivers a short daily human-review queue with a written escalation policy that forbids acting on an unreviewed alert. That is a service business (install + calibration + monthly review support), not a product. The workflow and the local accountability are the moat; the detector and the NVR are commodity.

technical_approach.established_pattern: IP cameras -> local NVR running a person/object detector plus multi-object tracker -> zone and line-crossing rules per camera (each SCO lane, the bagging area, back door inside/outside, receiving dock, cash-wrap till) -> fusion with transaction events (POS export or SCO scan events) -> exception scoring and de-duplication -> short clip + still queued for human review -> reviewer confirms or rejects, and rejections feed back as training negatives. A small vision-language model is used only as a second stage on flagged clips (describe what is in the basket or hands, read a receipt or label), never as the primary alarm. This mirrors how published systems work: detection plus tracking to get stable person/object tracks, then a separate classifier over the track's trajectory or the POS-video comparison for lane-level events.

models_and_tools.name: Ultralytics YOLO (YOLO26 family) + built-in trackers
models_and_tools.role: Person and object detection and tracking. ByteTrack is the lightweight baseline (linear Kalman + IoU, no appearance model, no camera-motion compensation) and is the right default for static overhead cameras; BoT-SORT adds camera-motion compensation and optional ReID for moving cameras; TrackTrack is the current library default and targets crowded scenes with duplicate-ID problems.

models_and_tools.name: Frigate
models_and_tools.role: Local NVR, camera management, zones and review items, clip retention, MQTT/Home Assistant hooks. Ships with stock detectors and models, and its custom-model settings accept a model path plus a custom label map; item-level scan detection still has to be trained and wired by the integrator.

models_and_tools.name: Liquid AI LFM2-VL-450M / 1.6B
models_and_tools.role: Small vision-language check on flagged clips (e.g. 'is there an unscanned item in the bagging area?'), built for low-latency edge use; the model card recommends fine-tuning for narrow use cases and states it is not intended for safety-critical decisions - so it belongs in a review-assist role, not as the decision-maker.

models_and_tools.name: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct
models_and_tools.role: Stronger VLM when the store has a Jetson-class GPU and reviewer volume justifies it; official weights with transformers support, positioned by the vendor for edge-to-cloud deployment.

models_and_tools.name: llama.cpp (mtmd)
models_and_tools.role: Runs a VLM locally on the store box or a small GPU server with no cloud dependency, which keeps footage and inferences on site; Liquid AI publishes GGUF weights with llama-mtmd-cli usage examples for its 3B model.

models_and_tools.name: Cactus (optional)
models_and_tools.role: Runs text, speech and vision models locally with one Python package, with tool calling, structured extraction, transcription and fine-tuning documented in the README; the MLX-on-Apple-silicon path additionally exposes a local OpenAI-compatible server. Usable for a reviewer app that runs a small model on a manager's machine rather than shipping video to a cloud service.

hardware.item: Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit (8GB, 67 TOPS) - local inference box
Google Coral USB Accelerator (Edge TPU) - cheaper detection-only option
hardware.approx_cost: $59.99 list (often out of stock; resellers well above list)

hardware.item: Raspberry Pi AI Kit (M.2 HAT+ preassembled with a Hailo-8L, 13 TOPS)
PoE IP cameras (4K dome/bullet, 4-12 per store)
hardware.approx_cost: $100-200 each (inference from vendor store listings; Rhombus-branded equivalents list at $399 for the camera alone)

hardware.item: PoE switch, cabling, mini-PC/NVR storage, UPS
hardware.approx_cost: $400-900 per store (inference - not price-verified in this research)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Split answer. Zone, loitering, back-door and receiving rules need no fine-tuning - a stock person detector plus zones is enough, and Frigate will run either its bundled models or a custom model with its own label map. Item-level scan-bagging detection does need a custom detector trained on that store's own camera angles and packaging, plus per-store threshold calibration against a labelled week of footage; there is no off-the-shelf model that knows 'this box of cereal moved from hand to bag without a scan'. Frigate+ hosted training cannot help here because only a fixed label set is supported and custom labels cannot be added. Treat VLM prompting as configuration and VLM fine-tuning as a later optimisation, not a starting requirement.
technical_approach.data_needed: Two to four weeks of footage from the exact camera positions at the exact focal lengths; a POS export covering the same period (transaction-level if available, Z-reports at minimum); 500-3,000 labelled clips per camera scene, skewed to hard negatives (re-scans, hand-offs, kids, bags already in the cart, employee assistance); a documented exclusion list (uniforms, break areas, restrooms) and a named reviewer. Plan on relabelling after the first two weeks of live false positives.

measured_outcomes.finding: Self-checkout raises loss by a mean of 22% in year one (range 3.19%-41.2%), and by +0.26 percentage points of sales; regression on 4 case studies (3 retailers) puts the effect of each extra 1% of transactions through SCO at 0.030%-0.048% more shrink.
measured_outcomes.sample: 39 retailers overall (>EUR 1 trillion turnover); the before/after estimates rest on 19 before/after studies, with +22% from 8 grocery retailers / 1,300 test stores, +0.26pp from 11 grocery retailers / 1,700 test stores, and the per-1% regression on 4 case studies

measured_outcomes.finding: Interventions help but the evidence is thin: of 14 companies testing non-scan identification technology, 7 reported positive findings - one a 9% loss reduction, another $136m saved across 2,000 stores (0.13% sales increase), and one a reported 4.5x recovery of the initial outlay.

In live self-checkout data, 3%-10% of transactions generated a non-scan nudge or alert, and customers self-corrected after a soft nudge in 80%-97% of cases (a hard stop was needed in the remaining 3%-20%) - a direct warning that raw alert counts massively overstate theft.
measured_outcomes.sample: Nudge/alert rate: data from 2 retailers (one USA, one UK) and 2 vendors. Self-correction rate: data from 2 retailers.

measured_outcomes.finding: Average US shrink was 1.6% of sales ($112.1bn) with internal plus external theft about 65% of it; 53% of retailers increased technology and software budgets and 46% increased their use of third-party security personnel in response.

Facial-recognition alerts produced thousands of false matches over eight years and employees acted on them by following, searching, ejecting and calling police on innocent customers; the settlement banned facial recognition for five years and required notice, complaint handling and deletion.
measured_outcomes.sample: Hundreds of Rite Aid stores; FTC administrative action

measured_outcomes.finding: A YOLOv5 + Deep SORT pipeline that converts each person's bounding-box coordinates into a time series and classifies it with time-series models (XceptionTime, MiniRocket, InceptionTime, XCM) reached a 92% F1 on shoplifting clips from UCF-Crime, beating the RTFM baseline by 3 points and running 8.45x faster at inference.
measured_outcomes.sample: UCF-Crime shoplifting subset: 267 normal + 50 abnormal videos split into 544 clips (81 test clips, 14.9% abnormal). Benchmark video, not a live store.

measured_outcomes.finding: Sweethearting (cashier fake-scan) can be detected from checkout video: motion-based candidate generation produces primitive events at the point of sale, spatio-temporal features and Multiple-Instance-Learning models prune the falsely alarmed candidates, and transactions are validated by temporal ordering - demonstrated on data captured in a real grocery store.
measured_outcomes.sample: One real grocery store; conference paper, no field precision/recall or deployment metrics in the abstract

measured_outcomes.finding: Vendor-commissioned analysis claims a 374% three-year ROI (payback under six months, $88,000 recovered per store per year, 0.14% of covered-lane revenue) for checkout vision AI, with interviewed retailers reporting a $41,000-$260,000 per-store range.
measured_outcomes.sample: Forrester TEI composite of 4 interviewed retail leaders, modelled as a 200-store, $20bn-revenue grocery chain

legal_privacy.issue: Automated flags acted on by staff without safeguards can be an unfair practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC v. Rite Aid (Dec 2023): five-year ban on facial recognition in stores, mandated notice to consumers, written complaint investigation, deletion of images/algorithms, third-party assessments, CEO certification. The order is about biometric surveillance, but the reasoning (untested accuracy, no false-positive tracking, no employee training, disparate impact) maps onto any alert system staff act on (inference).

legal_privacy.issue: Biometric data collection carries separate FTC scrutiny even absent a state statute.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: FTC Policy Statement on Biometric Information (adopted 2023; the FTC announced it on 18 May 2023, reportedly on a 3-0 vote). The statement says false or unsubstantiated claims about biometric accuracy may violate the FTC Act and lists factors the Commission will weigh in judging unfairness, including failing to assess foreseeable harms before collecting, surreptitious or unexpected collection, failing to vet vendors and end users, failing to train employees, and failing to monitor the technology in use. A non-biometric design (no face templates, no voice prints, no gait ID) avoids that whole surface.

legal_privacy.issue: Recording audio of customers or staff conversations in the store.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act is described in secondary sources as one-party consent under N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d), with interception of a communication you are not a party to a third-degree crime under N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-3 - so a camera microphone recording conversations among customers or staff, with no participant consenting, is the exposure. I did not read the statutory text itself (the Justia copy returned HTTP 403), so this rests on a secondary summary that quotes the subsections and links the statutes; treat it as unconfirmed and the operational rule as absolute: disable microphones and record no audio.

legal_privacy.issue: Employee and customer privacy tort exposure for camera placement and review.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's intrusion-upon-seclusion tort, restated by the state Supreme Court in Friedman v. Martinez (2020), turns on intrusion into a private space plus conduct highly offensive to a reasonable person; the Court tied the tort to the placement of a surveillance device in an area reasonably expected to be private rather than to proof of viewing. Sales floors, checkouts, back rooms and loading docks are defensible; restrooms, changing areas and break rooms are not.

legal_privacy.issue: Is there a New Jersey statute requiring notice or signage for ordinary retail/workplace cameras?
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: I could not confirm one. A secondary survey states there is no New Jersey statute requiring notice or signs for ordinary workplace video cameras, and that N.J.S.A. 34:6B-22 (electronic tracking notice, civil penalty up to $1,000 for a first violation and $2,500 for later ones) covers only a tracking device in a vehicle used by an employee. Posting signage is therefore a policy choice and a liability reducer, not a verified legal mandate - though under N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9(d) a posted prior notice plus a lawful purpose is an affirmative defence to the invasion-of-privacy offences, which is a reason to post anyway.

legal_privacy.issue: Criminal exposure for cameras in private areas.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9 criminalises observing, recording or disclosing images of exposed intimate parts or sexual activity without consent where a reasonable person would not expect to be observed, and a retail store gets a notice carve-out only for the fitting-room entrance/access way (2C:14-9(e)(1)), never inside a stall (2C:14-9(f)). Secondary summary quoting the statute; I did not read the statute text.

NLRB General Counsel Memo GC 23-02 (31 Oct 2022) is prosecutorial guidance, not a Board holding: it urges the Board to find a presumptive Section 7 violation where an employer's surveillance and management practices, viewed as a whole, would tend to interfere with protected activity, and to require employers to disclose the technologies used, why, and how the data is used (absent a business need for covert use). Practical implication: no covert cameras aimed at organising activity, no using alerts to punish protected concerted action, and a written policy on what the system is and is not used for.

legal_privacy.issue: State privacy-statute exposure in New Jersey (biometric and otherwise).
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: The New Jersey Data Privacy Act (P.L. 2023, c.266) treats 'genetic or biometric data that may be processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying an individual' as sensitive data, but expressly excludes photographs, audio/video recordings and data generated from them unless generated to identify a specific individual - which is exactly the line a non-biometric design stays behind. It applies only to controllers processing personal data of at least 100,000 consumers in a year (excluding data processed solely to complete a payment transaction), or at least 25,000 consumers while earning revenue from selling personal data; 'consumer' excludes a person acting in a commercial or employment context, so employee footage is largely outside it. The statute takes effect on the 365th day following enactment.

legal_privacy.issue: False accusation, defamation and false imprisonment risk when staff act on an alert.
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: No New Jersey statute or appellate case I found squarely governs AI-alert-driven accusations. The FTC complaint documents the harm pattern (public accusation, search, police call) that would ground tort claims; treat this as unconfirmed legal analysis (inference), not a cited precedent. Note the statutory shield in N.J.S.A. 2C:20-11(e) protects a merchant who detains or causes arrest on probable cause - an unreviewed algorithmic flag is not the same evidentiary basis as an observed concealment (inference).

I found no New Jersey statute setting a retail video retention period. Recommendation is a contractual policy (e.g. 30 days rolling, exceptions exported and held with a case note), role-based access, and deletion on request from the store owner - this is a design choice (inference), not a legal requirement I could confirm.

public: Self-checkout lanes visible in Google Maps/Street View or store photos, especially 4+ lanes with one attendant.
Job postings for 'self-checkout attendant', 'overnight receiving', 'loss prevention associate' or 'asset protection' at a single-site independent.
Google/Yelp reviews that mention being asked for receipts, waiting for an attendant, or items not scanning (inference: indicates SCO friction and unattended lanes).
Recent local police blotter or news items naming the store or its block for shoplifting.
Store assortment: spirits on open shelves, OTC, power tools, infant formula, energy drinks - categories NRF names as organised-retail-crime targets.
Number of locations and rough square footage from the operator's own site (a 2+ store independent can amortise the build across sites).
Old analog/dome cameras visible outside and no camera over the loading door (inference from street-level photos).
Public liquor-licence and business-registration records (NJ ABC / county) to size the operator and confirm ownership structure.
walk_in: Count self-checkout lanes vs attendants at peak; note whether the attendant also covers customer service or the cigarette case.
Look for a camera directly over each SCO bagging area and over the cash-wrap till; absence is the sale.
Back door: is it propped, alarmed, on a camera, and is there a dock/count station with light?
Receiving practice: does anyone count cases against the invoice, or is it 'sign and stack'?
POS terminal type (Square, Clover, NCR, Lightspeed, legacy) and whether the manager can export transaction-level data.
Existing DVR/NVR brand and age, where the monitor sits, and who actually reviews footage (often: nobody).
High-theft SKU placement: razors, spirits, formula, OTC, tools - locked cases are a signal of prior loss pain.
Staffing and turnover: single clerk overnight, new faces weekly, posted schedules (inference: higher internal-theft and sweethearting risk).
Cash controls: who closes, how often drops happen, whether refunds/voids require a second person.

pilot.scope: One store, 4 weeks live after a 1-week install/calibration. Four to six cameras: two overhead on self-checkout/checkout lanes, one inside the back door, one outside the back door or on the receiving area, one on the cash-wrap/till. Local NVR and inference box on the store network; no audio; signage at the entrance stating cameras are in use for loss prevention and that alerts are reviewed by staff. Daily POS export ingested overnight (transaction-level if the POS allows, otherwise the Z-report plus void/refund/no-sale log). Output is a reviewer queue only: every alert is a short clip plus a still, marked 'unverified', and the written policy forbids staff approaching, searching or accusing anyone on the basis of an alert. Weekly 30-minute review with the owner on precision, alert volume and false-positive themes; alert types that fail precision are switched off, not tuned forever.
pilot.hardware: 4-6 PoE 4K cameras, PoE switch, Jetson Orin Nano Super (or Coral/Hailo if detection-only), 2-4 TB storage, UPS, small network cabinet. Reuse the store's existing cameras if they are IP and at least 1080p with a clean overhead view of the bagging area.
pilot.success_metric: Precision and workload, not 'theft stopped': (1) at least 60% of alerts confirmed as genuine exceptions on human review by week 4; (2) total alerts under ~15 per day so a manager can clear the queue in under 20 minutes; (3) zero alerts that led to a customer confrontation; (4) at least one documented, clip-backed exception per week in each of the three target categories (SCO non-scan, back-door/receiving, cash-wrap). Dollar shrink impact needs a full inventory cycle and is explicitly out of scope for a 4-week pilot.
pilot.cost_range: Roughly $5,000-$9,000 one-time plus $250-$500/month support for a single store. Assumptions: 4-6 cameras at $100-200 each ($400-1,200); compute and storage $600-1,200; switch/cabling/UPS $400-800; install and aiming 16-24 hours at $100-150/hr ($1,600-3,600); POS ingestion and rule/zone calibration 20-40 engineering hours ($2,000-4,000 at internal cost or a discounted pilot rate); monthly covers remote health checks, model/threshold updates and the weekly review call. Excludes the owner's own staff time, any POS vendor fees, and a Frigate+ commercial licence if hosted training were used (inference-based estimate, not a quoted price).
pilot.assumptions: Store already has a working network and at least some IP cameras; POS can export transaction or Z-report data at least daily; one named manager owns the review queue; no facial recognition, no audio, no cloud video by default; pilot pricing is discounted and hardware is resold at cost plus install margin; no claim of measured shrink reduction is made until a full inventory cycle is compared.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is well documented (1.6% shrink across 177 brands; mean +22% loss after self-checkout across 8 grocery retailers within a 19-study before/after set) but it is chain-weighted, so 16 of 20. Local buyers exist in volume - 2,280 retail establishments in Middlesex County - but most are small and many run few or no SCO lanes, so 11 of 15. Ability to pay is the weakest commercial factor: county retail average pay of $45,485 and $30,985 in liquor stores implies thin margins, and a $5-9k pilot plus $250-500/month is a real decision, hence 8 of 15. Technical feasibility is only moderate (10 of 20) because item-level scan detection needs POS event fusion and per-store custom training, while zone and back-door rules are easy. Legal risk scores 6 of 15: the non-biometric, review-only design removes the biggest hazard (the Rite Aid fact pattern) but leaves live Section 5 exposure if staff act on untested flags, defamation/false-imprisonment risk on any accusation, wiretap exposure if any audio is captured, NLRB scrutiny of employee monitoring, and a New Jersey notice/signage gap I could not close with a verified statute. Defensibility is 6 of 15: Frigate, YOLO and small VLMs are commodity, and Rhombus/Everseen can move downmarket; the durable position is local install plus POS integration plus a disciplined human-review workflow and escalation policy - a service moat, not a model moat. Sub-scores sum to 57 of 100.

risks: False positives leading to a customer accusation: the exact harm pattern the FTC charged Rite Aid over. Mitigation (review-only queue, no confrontation, written policy, signage) must be contractual, not aspirational.

Employee-relations blowback: staff read 'alert system' as suspicion. NLRB GC 23-02, though only guidance, signals scrutiny of intrusive monitoring; announcing purpose and limits before switch-on is safer than a surprise rollout.

POS integration is the real project risk. Independents often run Square/Clover with limited exports, or a legacy POS; without transaction-level data, scan-bagging detection degrades to person-in-zone analytics.

Licensing traps: Ultralytics Free/Pro plans are listed as AGPL 3.0, so a closed commercial deployment points to the Enterprise licence (reading, not legal advice); and Frigate+ training supports only a fixed label set while its terms forbid deploying the models at customer sites, so an installer bundling Frigate+ models needs a commercial licence.

Commodity competition: Rhombus-class cloud cameras at $399 hardware + $149 licence per camera keep improving, and at the Professional tier that licence excludes the AI features - a local integrator must sell judgement and workflow, not just detection.

Store economics: a $5-9k pilot plus $250-500/month has to be justified against a shrink number most independents do not measure precisely - expect long sales cycles and requests for proof from a neighbouring store.

Chain-of-custody and evidential quality: if clips are handed to police under New Jersey's upgraded retail-theft law, timestamp integrity, retention logs and access records need to be right. Note that the merchant probable-cause shield in N.J.S.A. 2C:20-11(e) presumes actual probable cause, which an unreviewed algorithmic flag does not establish (inference).

Scope creep into HR: owners will ask the system to police employee breaks and productivity, which converts a loss-prevention tool into continuous employee monitoring and raises the legal and cultural risk sharply.
caveats: Shrink and self-checkout statistics come from large-chain surveys (NRF's 177 brands; ECR's 39 retailers, with individual figures resting on 2-19 studies or retailers) - I found no New Jersey-specific or small-independent shrink rate, so applying 1.6% and +22% to a Milltown store is an inference, not a measurement. All vendor outcome claims (Everseen's 374% ROI, the $88,000 per store, and the ECR-reported 9% loss reduction/4.5x return that came from retailers themselves) are Low strength: vendor-produced, Forrester-modelled or self-reported. The ECR nudge/self-correction figures rest on 2 retailers plus 2 vendors and are rated Low. Peer-reviewed detection accuracies (the 92% F1 benchmark result, the sweethearting method) are benchmark or single-store results, not live small-store performance. Pricing for Everseen, NCR, Solink, Agilence and Frigate+ is not published and is listed as Unknown; Rhombus and Ultralytics list prices are MSRP/list as of the pages opened. Hardware prices are list prices at time of research and vary by reseller and stock; the Hailo-8L inside the $70 Raspberry Pi AI Kit is not priced separately in the source used. Nothing here is legal advice: the confirmed items are agency actions, one state Supreme Court opinion and statutes I read, and every 'confirmed: false' item is flagged where I relied on secondary summaries or on inference.
data_gaps: No New Jersey or Middlesex County shrink rate specific to independents; NRF and ECR data are chain-weighted.
